utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone after a recess slightly longer than we had in mind when we left this courtroom last year. This was caused by a request of the Defence to have additional time to study the Mladic diaries. Yes, Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to briefly deal with a few procedural matters. I'm also informed that the parties would like to raise some procedural matters as well. I'll try to go through it as quickly as possible without challenging the capacities of our interpreters and transcriber. First, I'd like to read out a request which is the following: This is a request for information from the parties on matters related to the further scheduling of this case. While the Chamber is well aware that there are a number of pending issues that may make it difficult for the parties to accurately predict the future scheduling, the Chamber nonetheless views it as important that some sort of time-frame be set, in order to give all parties and the Chamber an idea of what to expect. The Chamber therefore requests the Prosecution and each Defence team to make brief submissions on the following five questions, and the submissions should be filed no later than the 2nd of February: Firstly, the Prosecution is asked to inform the Chamber on what dated it expects to close its case. Secondly, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber if they intend to make submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and if so, how much time they would require for the actual submissions. Thirdly, the parties are asked to inform the Chamber on how many working days they would require between the closure of the Prosecution's case and a possible first hearing for Rule 98 bis submissions. Fourthly, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber on how many working days they would require between the last day of Rule 98 bis submissions, if any, and the start of the Defence case, if there is a need to present one. Fifthly, and finally, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber, provided that there is a need to present a case, in which order they would like to present their evidence. In it's planning, the Chamber will do its utmost to take the parties' wishes into account. And this concludes the Chamber's request for information. Second item I'd like to deal with is related to Witness JF-051. The OTP, in an e-mail of the 16th of December to the Simatovic Defence, has announced that it would drop the evidence of Witness JF-051. As a consequence of this information, the Chamber declares moot, A, the Prosecution's motion for admission of further written evidence of Witness JF-051 pursuant to Rule 92 ter, which was filed on the 28th of August, 2008; B, an OTP request for an in-camera examination on protective measures which dates the 22nd of June, 2010. Further, the Chamber declares moot the Prosecution motion for the admission of the diary of JF-051 pursuant to Rule 94(B) which was filed confidentially on the 19th of July, 2010. In relation to that last motion, I put on the record that the Stanisic Defence responded to this motion on the 2nd of August, 2010, that the Prosecution then on the 6th of August, 2010, filed a request for leave to reply to the Stanisic Defence, and the Chamber granted the Prosecution leave to reply, and informed the parties by way of an e-mail on the 19th of August. This was all not yet on the record. It is now, but that doesn't change that the Chamber has declared the motion moot. I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On the 12th of January, the Stanisic Defence has informed the Chamber through an informal communication that it had decided not to request a re-call of Witness JF-056 for further cross-examination. We have not received any request from the Simatovic Defence for further cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Simatovic Defence -- well, I don't know, we have informed the OTP and the Chamber that we are giving up on a witness that we thought we might re-call for cross-examination, yes, it's JF-052. But as far as JF-056, that's fine; we don't want to re-call him either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Victims and Witness Section is hereby instructed to inform the witness that the instruction that was given to him not to speak to anyone about his testimony is hereby lifted. Next matter. On the 10th of January, 2011, the OTP has informed the parties that it would not call Witnesses JF-055 and JF-028. This information was also included in the weekly notification to the parties on witnesses. As a result, the Chamber hereby declares the 92 ter motions for Witnesses JF-055 and JF-028 moot. Next matter. On the 10th of November, you, Mr. Jordash, objected to the Prosecution's line of questioning of Witness JF-004 based on lack of notice and in relation to voice recognition of Stanisic. At the end of the cross-examination on the 11th of November, you've asked to keep the cross-examination open in order to consult a voice recognition expert. Mr. Jordash, I hereby put on the record, on the 24th of January, you have in an informal communication informed the parties that you would see no need anymore to keep the cross-examination of Witness JF-004 open, and for that reason, hereby the Victims and Witness Section is instructed to inform Witness JF-004 that the instruction given to him that he should not speak to anyone about his testimony is hereby lifted. Then I would like to deliver a statement on behalf of the Chamber; it is the Chamber's statement with regard to an amended sitting schedule in the present case. On the 6th of December, 2010, the Chamber invited the reporting medical officer, the two independent medical experts, and the parties to make submissions on the possibility of increasing the number of sitting days from three to four days per week. These submissions were all filed in December 2010. On the 12th of January, 2011, the Prosecution informally notified the Defence and the Chamber of its schedule of witnesses for the remainder of its case. According to this schedule, the Prosecution expects to close its case, as far as the hearing of witnesses is concerned, around mid-February 2011, after only a few more weeks of court sessions. Under these circumstances, the Chamber has decided, for the moment, not to further pursue the option of increasing the number of sitting days per week. The Chamber will continue to sit three days per week throughout the remainder of the Prosecution's case, with the possibility of exceptionally increasing the sitting days if the scheduling of witnesses should require this. The Chamber may return to this issue at a later stage should there be a Defence case. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. Last item I would like to raise. On the 16th of December of last year, the Chamber admitted into evidence the previous testimony of witness Babic as public exhibits. Out of an abundance of caution, the OTP is requested to verify that no parts of the previous testimony are still subject to protective measures and report to the Chamber by Friday this week. These were the matters. I have one left, but in view of the time, I would prefer to deal with that one at a later stage. I was informed that the parties would like to raise certain issues. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an application with respect to the protective measures of the next witness that I would ask that we go into private session for me to address the Chamber on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome, any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The matter I'd like to raise is not a matter that I need to deal with at length right now but it is a matter which has become urgent and I'm seeking guidance from Your Honours as to when I can address you at some length on the issue. In a nutshell, the issue is that I am now without co-counsel, working co-counsel, I should say. And that is the result of funding inadequacies in this case arising from two directions: Principally, one, OLAD under-funding; and, two, also as a result of a partial indigency order and the client having no further money. We haven't in this Defence team resources to fund a second counsel. Now, it will take some time to outline precisely how we arrived at this situation. It has been a situation which has existed for many months but has been handled largely by, as Your Honours and the parties may have observed, myself conducting all the cross-examinations and effectively, in large part, playing the part of two counsel. We have outstanding applications with both the president of this Court and with OLAD; the first seeking an overturning of the indigency decision, the original indigency decision, and the second seeking OLAD's more reasonable assessment of the required funding of this case. That was filed on the 19th of November and as yet we still -- we have received no answer. The long and short of it is that there is absolutely no way the funding in this case for the Stanisic Defence can possibly fund two counsel, with one caveat; with the caveat that we fund ourselves and a P2 or P3 level. And as far as I'm concerned and as far as Mr. Knoops, who is the co-counsel on record is concerned, that is completely unacceptable. And so I'm raising it at this point. It's an issue of fair trial rights. And that's why we seek to bring it before the Trial Chamber. It's an issue of how this case can proceed. It is one thing to manage during the Prosecution case with only partial assistance of a co-counsel; it's another thing to manage during a Defence case, which, as I know from experience, is a much more labour-intensive endeavour. And in my respectful submission, it is simply not possible to do what we have to do over the next few months without additional funding and without additional counsel. I don't want to take the Court's time up at the moment, because I appreciate the delicacy of these next witnesses, and I simply raise it at this point. I would ask the Court to give me 30 minutes at some point over the next few days to lay out precisely what the problems have been, precisely what the consequences are for our ability to prepare for the Defence, and precisely what we will be seeking at this stage as a remedy. Those are my immediate submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Any further matter? The Chamber, of course, will consider your request, and I take it that the matter is important enough that we hear, either in the way you suggest or in any other way, any submissions, or read any submissions. It could well be that the Chamber for obvious reasons might want to inform itself about how matters at this moment are proceeding, apart from the fact that the primary responsibility for these matters is not with the Chamber, although it may result in any secondary responsibility. That's what you hinted at, I take it. Would there be any problem if the Chamber already would inquire as to where matters are getting stuck at this moment so that we at least show a keen interest in matters, in whatever direction, to be resolved, rather than to be on our desk for another half a year. I mean, we could ask OLAD, When do you think that what -- do you think that the matter could be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They've indicated that the issue of the monthly allowance, which is the principal problem, will be dealt with by the end of the week. They've separated that issue from the issue of the employment of a co-counsel and have indicated they'll respond to that in due course. Without getting into -- further into the argument, we would invite the Trial Chamber to make whatever inquiries Your Honours felt could properly apprise yourself of the issues. We -- it is a complicated issue, because the funding policy of OLAD is almost impenetrable, to my mind at least, and it has a lengthy history. Now, I do not expect to be able to lay it all out orally because it is that complicated, but -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that. And the only thing I was inquiring with you is that if we would seek further practical information. Because I think it would be appropriate that we would first listen to you before seeing whether there would be any -- any reason why we should go into the subject matter, which is of course something different from just knowing as to how to proceed and how matters stand. And we would do that in full transparency so in order not to get mixed up in our various positions: the one is outsiders, where we are not competent to decide on certain matters; and to the other extent being insiders, that we are the Guardians of the fair trial rights of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, do you have any matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we are discussing the matter with the Registry, I would kindly ask you to raise a problem of our financing. We have problems with resources, especially we've had those problems over the past two months, January and February. The -- it remains unknown where our Defence will be funded from. I didn't have anything special to add to this discussion, but since we are talking about your discussions with the Registry and since you have kindly promised to raise the issue of the other Defence, I would kindly ask you to raise the issue of our Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, we are not going to the merits at this stage; we are primarily looking at what the direct impact, practical consequences, of these discussions are. But I notice that apparently the financial creases has not missed to enter this courtroom, although rather late. Any other matter? If not, then I suggest to the parties that we would move into closed session in order to hear the evidence of the next witness. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My staff reminds me that if we would ever want to lift the closed session, whether we would just satisfy ourselves with the transcript or whether we would have to put face and voice distortion as an additional measure which would grant more flexibility at a later stage, whether we should put face and voice distortion in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't ask the witness that specific question, but from my discussions with him, I think he was thinking more in terms of the transcript; he felt that that gave him the protection. I think he may -- we can ask him when he comes in, but I think he may still have significant concerns with face and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I earlier introduced the matter with the Defence teams in terms of making the transcript public. They agreed with that. Mr. Groome now seems to -- that he would like to persist by that proposal. If there's any change of your minds, then I'd like to hear it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We leave it to the Trial Chamber's discretion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, we'll consider during the first break whether for the sessions after that we would -- because it would require at this moment a preparation of some 20 minutes to put especially the voice distortion in place --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was the original protection. I believe I can see the setup here now, so it may be immediately available, if the Chamber wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I spent too many words without thinking thoroughly and informing myself properly. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-030, in light of the protections that the Chamber has extended to you, I will refer to you throughout my examination as JF-030. I do know that you are fluent both in English and Serbian; which language would you prefer to testify here in today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can use any of the two. Is it possible for me to use Serbian when examined by the Defence, and when I'm examined by yourself, I would like to use English; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, as a matter of fact, if you'd say you would prefer direct communication with the person who examines you by using the same language, if that's your preferred choice, then I think there's no reason not to follow that. I would like to add two things: First, whenever you feel, even if you are speaking English, that you have difficulties in expressing yourself in that language and that you would rather rely on your mother tongue, that -- please indicate and change the language, but give our interpreters an opportunity to make that switch with you. Second, if you use the same language as the person that examines you, then there is a risk that direct response will cause difficulties for our interpreters. So you're invited both when examined in English, but also once you'll be examined in B/C/S, that you make a break, a small pause, between question and answer. And counsel will demonstrate how to do that. Isn't it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-030, did you, JF-053, myself, and investigator Gary Selsky have a brief meeting last evening after you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during this meeting -- and during this meeting, did you inform me that while you remain reluctant to give evidence in this case because of security concerns, it is your intention here today to answer questions that myself, the Defence, or the Trial Chamber may put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-030, in order to expedite your testimony here today, it is my intention to tender three documents containing your evidence. First a statement signed by you and provided in August of 2003, identified as 65 ter 5771. Second, on 14 September 2009, you reviewed your 2003 statement and informed Thomas Evangelos, an OTP staff member, of corrections you wished to make. I will seek to tender his notes from that review, identified as 65 ter 5855. And finally, in November of 2007, you met with another member of the OTP by the name of Klaus Hoffmann and provided additional information to him, which he recorded in a memorandum dated the 15th of February, 2008, identified as 65 ter 5851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I ask you, the September 2009, you identified them as 65 ter 5855; however, on a sheet we received, it is 5255.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is the mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- apologise; that was a typographical error that I should have corrected in advance of my testimony [sic]. The correct 65 ter number in e-court is 5855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That, then -- yeah, it's clear to me. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During our meeting yesterday evening, did I provide you with a copy of these three documents and ask that you review them prior to coming to the court here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, review these documents last evening and this morning and inform me that there were some changes you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I told that there's some details in the -- in this statement what was written by Mr. -- the German guy I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to take these in order and then we can address any corrections you wish to make in an orderly fashion. I would first like to deal with your 2003 statement and the corrections that you advised Mr. Evangelos of in September 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 5771 be called to the screens before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if you look to the screen, or the screen on your right, in a few moments you should see 65 ter 5771. I can see that it is now being displayed. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That goes without saying when we are in closed session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this your 2003 statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that your signature in the line with "witness" written below it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time could I ask that 65 ter 5855 be called to our screens. It is an information report dated the 14th of September, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While we are waiting for both versions to be shown to us, can I ask you, since you do speak English, what was the language that you worked in and that you reviewed in advance of your testimony? Did you work with the English version or did you work with the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that time, it was Mr. Garry Selsky -- actually, not. In the 2003, it was -- it was Mr. Kaizer Rizvi. And on that time I was communicate and I was giving the statement in English to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you reviewed that in advance of your testimony today, did you review the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I review English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to 5855, which is now on our screen, can I first ask you, are these the notes of Mr. Evangelos recording corrections to your 2003 statement that I asked you to review before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you -- there are two versions on our screens; which is the version that you reviewed for the purposes of this exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I review both of them and I saw there was some missed points, some differences, because whoever was doing the translation, he didn't translate it from English to B/H/S [sic] as I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So which should the Chamber consider the authoritative version, the more reliable version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after having reviewed the English version of 5855, did Mr. Evangelos accurately record the corrections and clarifications you wished to make to your 2003 statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we return for a moment to 65 ter 5771 and to paragraph 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being called up, perhaps I can refresh your recollection. That paragraph describes events surrounding the NATO bombing of Serbia in March of 1999. You provide information about people you describe as Frenki's Men and say: "They were putting on musk," m-u-s-k. Can you describe for us what you meant to say in paragraph 89? What were the men putting on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mask what usually using -- actually, this is like a -- like a -- or to put on the face, to cover your face, like Special Forces and other, let's say, police units, not to be recognised by their faces in publicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall the colour of that mask or those masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, usually it's black. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are there any other corrections you wish to make to your 2003 statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so there is nothing there to be -- to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that 65 ter 5851, an information report authored by Klaus Hoffmann and dated the 15th of February, 2008, be brought to our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last document I'd like to deal with this afternoon is a report that an OTP staff member Klaus Hoffmann drafted in February 2008, after speaking with you on the 14th and 15th of November 2007. I'd ask you to look at the document on your screen. It is currently identified as 65 ter 5851. Are these the notes of Mr. Hoffmann that I asked you to review in advance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After reviewing this document, did you have a number of corrections you would need to make to Mr. Hoffmann's notes in order for them to accurately reflect your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This morning did you identify for me the paragraphs you wished to either change or add text to before you adopt this document as accurately reflecting your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The most orderly way that we can proceed is the following: I will draw your attention to each paragraph you indicated you wished to make a change to, and I would ask the usher to display that paragraph on the screen before you. When we all can see the paragraph on the screen, would you please tell us what amendments you wish to make to that paragraph and that paragraph only. Once we have finished with a paragraph, I will advance until we come to the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we first look at paragraph 4, which is on the screen presently in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please tell us, after you have refreshed your recollection by reading it, what, if any, changes you wish to make to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would also say there would need to be a minor change also in the number 3, paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please tell us what that change would be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Here is stated that it was necessary to get a recommendation from DB for any post, even in the SJB. In Yugoslavia it was always necessary, whenever somebody were applying to get a job in the state institutions, need to have a good recommendation which was done by the service people who were taking the acknowledge about the person on the ground, on the field, to find out who he is, is he okay or not, his family, et cetera, et cetera. On that time also was very interested political, also, orientation of the people; so if you were politically, let's say, okay, and you have a good background and family good background, they were giving recommendation, and this recommendation was always accepted and requested, actually. To get the good position, good job, and the responsible position, you needed have this kind of recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to paragraph 4, what, if any, changes do you wish to make to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. In the paragraph number 4 it is stated that Ilija Kojic, Milan Milanovic, aka Mrgud, from time to time they went to Belgrade to report directly to Stanisic. I didn't say this, that, and I wouldn't say this, directly to Stanisic, because they went to Belgrade. They didn't say to me, Okay, we are going to Stanisic. But they went to Belgrade to give the report about the situation, about the needs on the fields, what was necessary about standard things. And they went to Belgrade for, let's say, giving the report to the people who are on top, who can make the decision and who can give the further instructions what to do, how to do it, I mean, who were on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now can I draw your attention to paragraph 5. That was a paragraph you indicated that you wanted to add some information to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During that time it was territory of Yugoslavia, and it was some intention of necessities to cut the part of Yugoslavia. And the people who were deployed on the fields, they were supposed to get the salaries. And that salaries, it's normally coming -- came from Belgrade, from capital, for -- to pay people who were deployed to -- to that area. So it was normal situation during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could advance to paragraph 12. Looks like we may have gone too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if anything, would you want to change in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, here it's stated that I was saying that Red Berets, a unit in Ilok under the direct command of the Serbian DB and Frenki Simatovic. I would change this. It was on that time the Red Berets were formed by the instruction of Badza Stojicic, and on that time, as I know, my knowledge is that Frenki was not involved in this, that meaning Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you wish to change to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was also stated here that Arkan was responsible in reporting only to Stanisic. I never said like this. Arkan was -- whatever he was doing, he was giving the report to the head of the -- of the -- of the responsible people in the state. That mean to DB or to whomever, but I never mentioned that he was under his command direct. And also this I would change: The name, this word "criminals," I would put there militants who were not -- they would not be easy to be controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are two -- that word is used twice in this paragraph, first in the second line. Which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, two times, yes. "Commander of criminals who could not be controlled." I would put: "The militants who could not be controlled."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what do you mean? How do you define militants?

utterances.text: Militants are the people who are extremists; it doesn't matter they are criminals or not. Therefore I would not put "criminals," because they were not everybody criminal who was there. Maybe there were some people with a criminal back or past, actually, a criminal past, but not to say criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Witness JF-030, the Chamber has heard that a lot of the changes you make, where you either say, "I haven't said that" or "I don't remember having said such a thing," are specifically where in your statement or in your -- in the report Mr. Hoffmann writes down that you referred to one of these accused. I would like to bring two things to your attention: First, that also in respect to these kind of changes, that you are bound by the solemn declaration you've given. Second, I would like to draw to your attention that if Mr. Hoffmann apparently in so many instances always wrote down what you did not say or what you don't remember to have said, that the Chamber might want to verify that and that we could, for example, inquire into whether there's an audio recording of that conversation you had or to ask Mr. Hoffmann to tell us more about it, and the Chamber will then have to consider, at least may consider, whether they would believe what is put on paper, perhaps after having heard Mr. Hoffmann on the matter, or whether we would believe your changes, which -- and, of course, we further have to analyse that -- which seems to show a certain pattern. And that's what I want to bring to your attention. So, your obligation to tell us what you remember, and also to inform you that we might further verify and that we may consider to use your statement also to the extent you have not attested to it. Of course, that would need further submissions by the parties, and we would have to carefully and cautiously consider that, but I just wanted to inform you about all this before we move to the next changes you had on your mind. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

utterances.text: No. Apparently -- could you -- I could not recognise the word in English. Could you please use the word in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. [Interpretation] They were not under -- or, rather, they were under the authority of the state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the matter, I think. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, finally, can I draw your attention to paragraph 44. What, if anything, do you wish to change in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I would say the same. The Red Berets were under the control of the DB, or the top of DB. Who was commanding, who was giving the orders, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-030, with these corrections, does this document, identified as 65 ter 5851, accurately reflect your evidence on the matters discussed with Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.text: If the Chamber considers the content of these three documents, identified as 65 ters 5771, 5855, and 5851, along with the corrections you have given testimony about today, do they have an accurate and truthful account of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: If I were to take the time to ask you the questions underlying this evidence here today, would you provide the same evidence in substance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May -- just one more thing. I remember I was giving some notifications somewhere else in this evidence but I can't remember on this moment which part of this I was giving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you one of two questions in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you would tell us what you think you told Mr. Hoffmann at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My position is that what I'm saying that I can't remember I was saying that. What I can remember during that time - as I says, during that time I was also not in the good health condition, and when they met me I was under the fever, et cetera, et cetera - what I can remember from that time, I know that approximately, approximately, I can

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there are two issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you now say is what your recollection is at this moment, and the second issue is what your recollection is as far as what you told Mr. Hoffmann. So what you actually are saying is: I have now recollection that I said something rather different from what Mr. Hoffmann put on paper. And, of course, that's not the first time you do that. There is in many respects. And very often if the names of the accused are at stake, you say: That's not what I said. So Mr. Hoffmann must have done a very bad job. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm putting it to you because it's the logical consequence of what you are telling us now. Is your recollection of what you said with Mr. Hoffmann, is it any more firm as what you tell us now that it's now your recollection that at the time you may have said something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the -- what I can remember. That is what I said, as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.text: But do you have any concrete facts concerning 1991 to 1995 to back this up, that this happened in practice rather than it being the norm prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any facts directly. I told you direct facts, I was this -- I was saying this as a -- in a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It happened prior to 1991; you assumed it continued to happen during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And before --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- you -- you assumed, because you had been told it happened before the war; and then you assumed, on the top of that, that it must have continued to happen between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, because it was to give --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it a presumption though?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could -- could the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to just give the brief explanation, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness finish his answer. You interrupted him, Mr. Jordash. Yes, you said you believed and then you wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Second World War, the communists took power in Yugoslavia, and you know that. And they were in Serbia, and still in Yugoslavia there were people who did not agree with this and they were monarchist, and they never agreed with that what happened. Therefore, if somebody in your family was a cousin or related to these kind of monarchists, et cetera, et cetera, it was not possible to get a good -- always possible position in the state. Up to now I hope so this stop over in Serbia and Yugoslavia, but during that time it was obviously. It was obviously. You have to have recommendation from MUP, that mean from DB, service, that you are okay, you have a good and clean background, and your dossier is clean so you can get a good position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know that this occurred in 1991 to 1995, or are you basing it on what you understood to be the general practice before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was before, and I believe so and I know so that it was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you believe or you know? I mean, what -- can you offer something --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for a matter of fact, actually, there was one period of time when they says they going to open the folders so everybody can see what was written for whom, et cetera, et cetera, so people found in their folders what exactly was written there even that was not truth. Because most of time, most of time, some of the people were subjective on the basis of this do they like somebody or don't like or do they belong to the family, which, during the Second World War, was collaborating with the monarchists, et cetera, et cetera, Chetniks, or police, or whatever. So if somebody wrote for you, for instance, for you some bad record, that was taken as a truth, nobody wouldn't dare to ask: Is this okay or not? It came from the top. It is in the records. Don't asking nothing, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have any concrete evidence that this occurred for any person in the SBWS between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Thank you. Paragraph 4. Did you say to Mr. Hoffmann: "The witness - with regard to his time in Eastern Slavonia - mentioned that Ilija Kojic and Milan Milanovic, aka Mrgud, from time to time went to Belgrade to report directly to Stanisic"? Did you say that sentence to Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I says previous, and I request this to be changed, that I know that they went to Belgrade to report --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But to report direct to Stanisic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you say that to Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that I say that went to -- direct to Mr. Stanisic to report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence about Mrgud reporting to Stanisic? No. Do you know why Mr. Hoffmann might have written that down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he asked me, Do you have any knowledge about these things, that -- what is going on, to whom they give reports? I says, yeah, I know that they have to go to report to Belgrade, to the superiors, and to get advice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you ask the witness why he did write that down, whereas the witness just changed, to some extent, his statement that he doesn't remember that he has said this to Mr. Hoffmann, there are two possibilities: either the witness doesn't remember but he said it, or he didn't say it. Now, to ask the witness, who doesn't remember whether he said it or not, at least not clearly, his recollection at this moment is that he would not have said it, but he retracted slightly when you put the question so clearly. Why could we then possibly ask this witness why Mr. Hoffmann did that? I can say two things: because he wanted to distort my statement, or he wanted to write down what I said. I mean, both speculation for the witness, who says I do not remember. And you may have noticed a slight difference. Did you say that to Mr. Hoffmann: "I can't remember that I said went direct to Mr. Stanisic." So the witness apparently has no firm recollection of not having said it, neither, certainly not of having said it. And that makes your question a bit speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the witness said he had no evidence about Mrgud reporting to Stanisic, which suggests that he wouldn't have said, if we take what the witness is saying as correct, as truthful, that he wouldn't have said that to Mr. Hoffmann. So I was exploring, then, why Mr. Hoffmann -- if the witness could offer any insight as to why Mr. Hoffmann might perhaps be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly the question I was -- there are so many ifs and ands in between that -- it's clear that the witness said he has no evidence on that. Sometimes people would say something even without having evidence, previous line of questioning is similar. Whereas I would not feed all the people who said that people were screened for more important state functions even without having evidence on that that's happening. So the fact that someone says something, even if he has no evidence on it, may well be the case and may even be frequently the case. But I was focusing on your question that this witness explained why Mr. Hoffmann did it. That's something -- unless you have good reasons to believe that he may have some insight in that, it's not a question you could reasonably ask from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, to be clear with the Court, Your Honour, it's not our case that Mr. Hoffmann did write this down from the top of his head. It's our case that the witness told him that. And now isn't able to substantiate it and he's retracting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then leave it to that, rather than ask the witness to speculate on why Mr. Hoffmann may have done what the witness considers he might have done but which you do not believe he has done. So that makes matters too complex. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if -- who Kojic went to see when he went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't say direct they go to see Mr. Stanisic or somebody as that. They always says they have to go to Belgrade to report, to give report, or to ask for something, for some needs, for some supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kojic or Mrgud never mention going to the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Ministry of Defence? I -- they says they have to go to Belgrade to superiors to request for help. On that time, they were going -- my -- that was -- I was hearing that they went to MUP and possible they -- I didn't hear for the Ministry of Defence in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because during that time, in the beginning, the military on the beginning was -- used to be like buffer zone between the two fighting sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They were -- Kojic and Mrgud were going to Belgrade to seek help; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They were not seeking instructions; they were seeking help. Help to, for example, form police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, they were seeking for help and supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Djordjevic worked for the public security of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did he report to in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did he report to in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have knowledge about these things. Because my -- what I know that they he have to deliver, further informations, whatever informations were collected in the fields, further delivered to the analytic service, and analytic service dispersed further to whom they need and to get. That is actually how this went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know whom he reported to in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Wasn't his superior Radovan Stojicic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- Badza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Djordjevic reported to Badza, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But there was no doubt in your mind, was there, that Badza was Djordjevic's superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: During 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Until the time of Badza's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then Djordjevic took over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, it's now for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pauses are asked for, and I thought you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I really apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take it into account. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When Badza was killed, Djordjevic took over as chief of the public security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I suggest that you did tell Mr. Hoffmann that you went several times to Belgrade for informal talks with Stanisic but you did so because you were trying to assist the Prosecution and you've changed your account now because you cannot substantiate that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm suggesting Mr. Hoffmann didn't make a mistake; you told Mr. Hoffmann, Mr. Hoffmann wrote it down, and now you've retracted it because it's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I says, I can't remember that I ever mentioned that I went to see Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to paragraph 9. No, we'll leave that one. Let's go to paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct you've retracted that Frenki Simatovic was involved with the Red Beret unit at Ilok, but you maintain that the Red Berets was a unit under the command of the Serbian DB; am I summing that up correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Red Beret were formed in Ilok on 1992. I didn't say that Mr. Simatovic was involved in this because it was direct initiative of Mr. Stojicic, Badza, and as I can remember, Zika Crnogorac was involved in this. But later on, the unit -- the unit become -- they move it -- them move them out to -- to Serbia, and then they were under -- under -- as a separate unit, as a war unit or whatever, they were under the control of DB. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And which time-period are you speaking of when you say "it became"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when they -- they were -- they were relocated from Ilok to -- I can't remember, actually, when they were relocated from Ilok to -- to Serbia. It was in Vojvodina. I can't really remember that. But during that -- during the time when they were in Ilok, they were controlled by Zavisic, and Badza Stojicic was coming there. There is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll return to that in a moment. When -- which year do you say they relocated to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember, I say. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, between 1991 and 1995 you cannot offer any insight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 199 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly reminded to break between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 1993. End of 1992 or -- I can't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I wrongly indicated to you that counsel would show you how to make pauses. But perhaps we should do it the other way around. You show Mr. Jordash how to make pauses between question and answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I apologise again to the translators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it's my fault. Can I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say they, at some point, became under the control of the DB, what precisely do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the DB was a relatively --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- large organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It could be under the command of part of the DB, the very top of the DB, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's say DB, as the name says, Drzavna Bezbednost, which mean the state security, they were formed to protect the state from any kind of, let's say, enemy inside, outside, et cetera, et cetera. That for [sic], the should have the top of the -- let's -- the people, equipment, and everything what was necessary to be for them. That for, I know that, and I believe so, the unit which was as a Red Beret formed from the people who are top trained for any anti-terrorist situations, et cetera, et cetera, I believe so and they should be under control of the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Arkan was responsibile in reporting only to Stanisic, Arkan was used by the Serbian DB, as a commander of criminals, could not be controlled otherwise. And you've changed or you've offered a clarification and you say you never said this, that he was reporting to Stanisic, but maybe the DB, but I never mentioned that he was under the direct command of Stanisic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, as I says, I changed this because this, my statement -- let me just to have a brief explanation. When I gave the statement, I sign it, it was Mr. Kaizer Rizvi there, and I didn't check it actually whatever was inside. I trust to Mr. Kaizer Rizvi, and I signed it and after that they informed me that my statement will never be used in these kind of -- in any case in Den Haag in front of the Court, and that for I didn't pay attention and I forgot most of things what he wrote there. As I says, I didn't read it carefully, the statement, I was just signing it. And that for when I read it again, when I came here and statement was given to me, then I request changes in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence that the -- that Arkan reported to anyone in the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Other than Stanisic, which you've now retracted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So do you you retract that then? That -- do you accept you don't know that Arkan reported to anyone in the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was saying, as I was saying on the beginning of the statement, that when Arkan came to Borovo Selo and from that time I believe so -- I was believing that he supposed to report and give the reports to the highest level command, and as I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Why do you say that's what he was supposed to report and give the reports to the highest level of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he -- when he arrived to Borovo Selo, as I was saying in the statement, he was saying he came from Belgrade, from the top level, he have instruction to help, to organise defence, and to protect the area from the attack of, let's say, separatists who were trying -- or who were killing the Serbians, and et cetera, et cetera. So as I says on the beginning of that statement, but furthermore, therefore, when I read the statement, I changed these things, and I -- I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But why, even today, do you say -- or did you try to link him to the Serbian DB? The top command in Belgrade could have been a number of groups, couldn't it, from Milosevic to Simovic, Ministry of Defence, to the federal Ministry of Interior, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could be. You're right. But, as I says, in -- in the state, such a thing to command, to have your own unit and to have full support in equipment and et cetera, whatever is necessary for that kind of unit, I don't think so without knowledge and suggestion of the DB that will be done. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Your Honour indicating the time? That that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was not, as a matter of fact. But we are 75 minutes past the moment when we started, so if this would be a suitable moment for you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, how often in 1991 did Stanisic see Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know how often he saw him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It was not part of my job to follow when they are going to meet and what they going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often do they speak on the telephone in the same period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many meetings did they have in the same period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Mr. Jordash wants to ask you is whether you have any factual knowledge on the frequency of any communications, direct or indirect, between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic. May I take it that your answer is that you have no factual information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash. I take it that you want to -- whatever is in the statement, that you then want to question that. But seven questions, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, that -- unless there's any reason to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to avoid compound questions. I was trying to break it down so there was no doubt and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed, let's proceed. I see your point. It's appreciated. At the same time, it can be done in a quicker way with the same result.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you -- do you know what Milosevic's view was concerning Mr. Stanisic and the role he played as chief of the state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you cannot say, can you, that Stanisic was below Milosevic and trusted by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's have a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you be so kind just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's have a look at paragraph 21 of -- let's call it the Hoffmann interview. P2093.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it says, "On the top was Milosevic and below him Stanisic, whom he trusted. Stanisic was very powerful ..." Do you accept that that is a conclusion you are not qualified to draw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, moving to the next assertion in paragraph 21 about Stanisic controlling the military intelligence. Now, you've withdrawn, or you say that's not what you told Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In fact, you'd go further than that and say, I'm fairly certain that that is not true, that I know of a conflict between the military and the civil intelligence; agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I says, I don't believe that Stanisic could control the military intelligence, could -- it was possible and it is possible that maybe he, Mr. Stanisic, have some people inside, I'm not, let's say, qualified to give this -- to be sure hundred per cent. But I didn't say there was a conflict, direct conflict, between the services because both of services they were working on protecting the country from the enemy, inside or outside, whatever. But it was like - I should say this on the B/H/S [sic] - [B/C/S spoken] [Interpretation] a rivalry [In English] between these two services --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- who is better. And therefore sometime there was some kind of things hidden from one or another side. But they were co-operating in the major, let's say, problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'd like one question, to be quite certain. Mr. Jordash asked you about paragraph 21, Mr. Stanisic controlling the military intelligence. Now, do you positively say, "I never said that to Mr. Hoffmann," or is it that you say, as you said at some earlier occasions, "I don't remember whether I said that to Mr. Hoffmann"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I says before, I don't remember that I say, but I don't believe. It was a question as I understood Mr. Jordash: Do you believe about the conflict between these; I says I don't believe that he, Mr. Stanisic, could control, completely, the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question is about whether you are positive that you did not say such words to Mr. Hoffmann, or is it, as you previously said at a couple of occasions, "I don't remember that I have said that"? That's different from, "I positively affirm that did I not say it." Which of the two is here the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I says, I can't remember that I says to Mr. Hoffmann these things. But furthermore, I was continuing that, saying I do not believe that Mr. Stanisic could control, completely, military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear and that was clear already. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We've had -- perhaps I'm being over-picky, Mr. Witness, but you've now slightly amended and you have repeated twice that you do not believe Mr. Stanisic could control, completely, the military. Are you now moving your position and saying he could control some of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Misunderstanding. He couldn't control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've had that belief since before 2008, haven't you? You believed he didn't or couldn't control it, prior to your interview with Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely. And before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have a look at paragraph 27 of this P2093, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "SDG was set up by Giska Bozovic in spring 1991, after the March demonstration in Belgrade." Did you say that to Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That I think so, yeah, I think so I did it, I told him this. Because there were discussion, reference to how the SDG was formed. I can remember that thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, you're saying the SDG, i.e., Arkan, what became known as Arkan's Tigers, was in fact set up by Giska Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the Arkan was commanding the Srpska Dobrovoljacka Garda, SDG, and Tiger Battalion was the name of his SDG. But on the beginning everybody knew it was SDG, Srpska Dobrovoljacka Garda.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Arkan, in spring 1991, according to you, had nothing to do with the SDG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And only came to have something to do with it in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know does he have anything to do with this, with the killing of Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, sorry, I'm ask -- if you look at the second-to-last, sorry the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "When he, Giska Bozovic, was killed in June 1991, (his deputy was killed as well at that time), the Serbian DB set Arkan on top of the SDG to be controlled by the DB."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't -- they didn't put him immediately. SDG, as I know that on that time, was not formed completely, because after killing Giska and his deputy, but later on. I didn't mention exact time that -- after 1991, that on that year the SDG was formed immediately by Arkan or was -- he come on top immediately after killing of Giska on the top of DB. I was not so precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take instructions please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Hoffmann that the Serbian DB set Arkan on top of the SDG to be controlled by the DB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the global conversation I was saying in the previous that the militants which come to Arkan, they were easy for control, because he was that one who was authority, a charismatic person, and they were listening to him. So therefore he was -- as I says, nobody cannot form such a unit to get a weapon and all equipment, military equipment, everything what is necessary, if he is not recommended by the highest level of the state, that mean from services as DB, military, whatever, but only because he was not -- under the control of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- one second. You are explaining --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you think now. The question was a different one. Mr. Jordash asked you: "Did you tell Mr. Hoffmann that the Serbian DB set Arkan on top of the SDG to be controlled by the DB." Is -- what Mr. Hoffmann wrote down, is that what you told him? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I was saying this. I was saying this in the -- in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer is yes to that. And if we need further explanations, then Mr. Jordash will certainly ask you for it. Mr. Jordash, there seems to be some opinion in those statements as well, if you want to explore that. This was not to cut you off, just to get a clear answer to the question you did put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even -- and don't be too concerned that this Chamber is usually able to distinguish between what is opinion and what is facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were offering an explanation, Mr. Witness, about why you'd come to that conclusion. And were you suggesting that you'd come to the conclusion that a unit such as Arkan's had to have authority from the highest level of the state, from the DB or the military or whoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. It's a military operative unit. A war operative unit, as I says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They cannot exist if there is not, let's say, support or permission from the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Otherwise it would be treated as a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think we can move on from that, if that's the basis of your conclusion about the DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, perhaps you think a bit about your next question because it's really time for a break. But before we do, I would like to adjourn in open session. So therefore, Witness JF-030, I hereby instruct you that you should not speak to anyone, and that includes family members. You should not discuss, communicate, in whatever way exchange any information about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear? Then I'll ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, after which we'll go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we adjourn, I'd like to inform the parties that where the Chamber has an opportunity to have one not-sitting week in the spring, that the Chamber at this moment is seriously considered to take that week, the week starting the 18th of April, which is the week before Easter, would then not sit until the 25th, Monday is then the Easter Monday. We would then resume on Tuesday, the 26th of April. That is what is on the mind of the Chamber at this moment. We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, the 26th of January, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom.
